title: 道德經 第三十九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 39, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 72. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 39 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 法本 (The Root as the Model). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.l: Of old, the ones that got the One:
sentences.n:
一, the One, is this chapter's word for the undivided — the same thing chapter 10 tells you to hold in both arms (抱一) and chapter 22 makes the sage's single grip. Wang Bi glosses it as the beginning of number and the utmost of things: one is where counting starts, and it is what anything must have to be a thing at all rather than a heap.

He also glosses 昔 not as 'long ago' but as 始, 'the beginning' — so the line may point at the first times rather than merely old ones. English 'of old' holds both, which is why it is what stands here.

者 is the workhorse of Classical Chinese: it turns whatever precedes it into 'the one(s) that…'. Here it builds a subject out of 昔之得一, and the six lines that follow unpack that subject one rung at a time.

sentences.t:
天得一以清，
地得一以寧，
神得一以靈，
谷得一以盈，
萬物得一以生，
侯王得一以為天下貞。
其致之，

sentences.i: Heaven, by attaining the One, is clear; earth, by attaining it, is settled; the spirits by it have their power; the valley by it is full; the ten thousand things by it are alive; lords and kings by it stand as the measure for all under heaven. This is what brings them about:
sentences.n:
Six members on one frame: X 得一以 Y — X got the One, and by it Ys. 以 ordinarily takes an object ('by means of X'), and here the object has simply been dropped, since it can only be the One; English has to put back the 'it' the Chinese leaves out. Expect that dropped object everywhere.

Hear this before you parse it: 清 qīng, 寧 níng, 靈 líng, 盈 yíng, 生 shēng, 貞 zhēn. All six belong to one Old Chinese rhyme group, and — unusually — most of the rhyme survives into Mandarin: only 貞 zhēn has drifted out of the sound the other five still share. This is one of the places where you can hear the poem as verse instead of taking a note's word for it.

The ladder is a cosmos in six rungs: sky, ground, spirits, valley, living things, rulers — and the rulers come last because they are the argument's real target. 神 is the numinous and 靈 is a spirit's efficacy, so 神得一以靈 comes close to 'the spirits got the One, and by it are spirit'. 谷, the valley, is one of the book's standing images (chapters 6, 15, 28): what is empty and low is what gets filled. 貞 begins as a divination word — the verdict read off a cracked oracle bone — and from there means steadfast, correct, true.

其致之 is three compressed characters, and we follow Wang Bi on them: his comment is that each thing gets this One and is thereby completed. So 其 is the One (the Chinese names no antecedent; supplying it is our choice), 致 is 'bring about', and 之 is the object pronoun pointing back at the six states just listed. The line can also be read 'press this to its limit', taking 致 in its other sense of carrying a thing through to the end; what follows — each rung with nothing left to work by — suits that reading too, and it is on the record here.

sentences.l: Heaven, with nothing by which to be clear, is like to split;
sentences.i: If heaven had nothing by which to be clear, the fear is that it would tear apart.
sentences.n:
There is no 'if' in this sentence. Classical Chinese sets down a topic — 天無以清, 'heaven, lacking what makes it clear' — and then comments on it, leaving the hinge to the reader. English cannot leave it out, so something has to be supplied.

將恐 is a doubled hedge rather than a prediction: 將 'is on the point of' with 恐 'it is to be feared'. And 裂 is the tearing of cloth — the sky rent from top to bottom.

This single line stands as a sense-unit by itself only because Wang Bi's commentary breaks in here, after the first member of the list; the five that answer it run on together in the unit that follows. We keep his cuts rather than invent our own, and this is a good example of how uneven they are.

sentences.t:
地無以寧將恐發，
神無以靈將恐歇，
谷無以盈將恐竭，
萬物無以生將恐滅，
侯王無以貴高將恐蹶。
故貴以賤為本，
高以下為基。
是以侯王自稱孤﹑寡﹑不穀。
此非以賤為本邪？非乎？
故致數輿無輿，
不欲琭琭如玉，
珞珞如石。

sentences.i: If earth had nothing by which to be settled, the fear is that it would give way; the spirits, nothing by which to have their power, that they would fall silent; the valley, nothing to fill it, that it would run dry; the ten thousand things, nothing to live by, that they would be snuffed out; lords and kings, nothing to be honoured and high by, that they would topple. And so what is honoured has what is base for its root, and what is high has what is low for its footing. That is why lords and kings style themselves the Orphan, the Scant One, the Un-good. Is that not making the base the root? Is it not? Count a carriage through, part by part, and no carriage is among the parts. Wish neither for the glint of jade nor for the knobbled rough of stone.
sentences.n:
The five failures answer the five attainments term for term, and they rhyme as hard as the first list did: 發 fā, 歇 xiē, 竭 jié, 滅 miè, 蹶 jué, with 裂 liè from the unit before. In Old Chinese these all ended in -t and made one rhyme group; five of the six still chime in Mandarin.

Then the pattern breaks, and on purpose. Where the first list gave the rulers 貞, the true measure, the second takes from them 貴高, 'honoured and high' — not the same thing at all. That swap is the hinge of the chapter: what the One gives a ruler is a standard to be, while what he stands to lose is only his elevation. Everything after this turns on the two pairs 貴/賤 and 高/下.

以…為… is the frame to learn here: 'take A as B, make A into B'. 貴以賤為本 is 'the honoured takes the base as root'. It runs through the whole book, and when 為 sits in this frame it is wéi, 'to make, to count as' — never wèi, 'for the sake of'.

孤, 寡 and 不穀 are not the book's coinages but the actual court language of the day: a feudal lord spoke of himself as 孤, 'the orphaned one', and as 寡人, 'the man of little'; the king styled himself 不穀, literally 'un-grain', where 穀 (the crop, what feeds people) had long since come to mean 'good'. The argument is that the rulers' own titles concede the point already, whatever their conduct does. Notice how a question is made: not by word order but by a particle at the end, 邪 and then 乎; and notice that a noun predicate is negated by 非, not by 不.

故致數輿無輿 is the hardest line in the chapter and the text is not secure. We follow the Wang Bi reading printed here, 輿 'carriage', and Wang Bi's own comment quotes the line back as 故致數輿乃無輿也 — tell a carriage over part by part, axle and box and spokes and yoke, and 'carriage' is nowhere among the parts. The carriage is what the low parts hold up, exactly as the honoured is held up by the base. Other editions read 譽 yù 'praise' in place of 輿 and take 數 as shuò 'again and again', which gives 'seek praise over and over and get no praise'. That is a real dispute and not a settled one; we take the crib we have and say so.

琭琭 and 珞珞 are rare doubled descriptives and their exact force is a guess — glossy and glinting for polished jade, knobbled and rough for raw stone. The commoner reading makes the last line a choice: not jade but stone. Wang Bi does not read it so; he says that jade and stone alike have their substance used up in how they look (體盡於形), so that neither is wanted. The single 不欲 governing both members is on his side, and that is the reading shipped here. The doubled question 非乎？ is left as the text prints it; we have not checked it against a manuscript apparatus, so nothing is claimed about how it got there.
